details:
**Persephone's abduction by Hades and the seasons**
Demeter's daughter Persephone (Kore) was kidnapped by Hades to be queen of the underworld. Demeter's grief as she wandered the earth searching for her caused a year-long famine, and because Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she must spend part of each year there; Demeter's mourning during those months explains winter.

**Demophon in the fire**
While searching for Persephone, Demeter, disguised as an old woman named Doso, became nurse to Demophon, the baby son of King Celeus and Queen Metanira of Eleusis. She anointed him with ambrosia and secretly held him in the hearth fire each night to burn away his mortality, but Metanira walked in and screamed, so the goddess revealed herself and the boy remained mortal.

**Pelops's shoulder**
When Tantalus cooked his son Pelops and served him to the gods, Demeter, distracted by grief over Persephone, was the only one who ate, consuming his shoulder. When the gods restored Pelops to life, he was given an ivory shoulder in its place, made by Hephaestus or by Demeter herself.

**Triptolemus**
A prince of Eleusis (in most versions the elder son of Celeus and Metanira) whom Demeter taught the secrets of agriculture in place of immortalizing Demophon. She gave him a winged chariot drawn by serpents (dragons), in which he flew around the world teaching people to plant grain.

**Eleusinian Mysteries**
The most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece, held at Eleusis in honor of Demeter and Persephone. Initiates drank the barley drink kykeon and were shown sacred objects (the hiera); one ancient source says the climax was the display of "an ear of wheat reaped in silence."

**Thesmophoria**
A festival for Demeter Thesmophoros ("Law-Bringer") and Persephone that only married women citizens could attend. Piglets were thrown into underground pits, commemorating the swineherd Eubouleus, whose pigs were swallowed by the earth along with Persephone when Hades took her; their decayed remains were later mixed with the seed grain.

**Erysichthon and Mestra**
Erysichthon, a Thessalian king, cut down a sacred grove of Demeter's, including a giant oak. Demeter cursed him with insatiable hunger; he sold his daughter Mestra again and again to buy food (she escaped each time by shapeshifting) and eventually devoured himself.

**Iasion and Plutus**
At the wedding of Cadmus and Harmonia, Demeter lay with the mortal Iasion in a thrice-plowed field. Zeus killed Iasion with a thunderbolt, and Demeter bore Plutus, the god of wealth (and in some versions Philomelus, linked to the constellation Bootes).

**Poseidon, Arion, and Despoina**
While Demeter was searching for Persephone, Poseidon pursued her; she turned into a mare and hid among the horses of King Onkios, but Poseidon became a stallion and mated with her. She bore the swift, talking horse Arion and the goddess Despoina ("the Mistress").

**Lyncus turned into a lynx**
Lyncus, a king of Scythia, tried to murder Triptolemus while he was a guest, in order to take credit for the gift of agriculture. Demeter turned Lyncus into a lynx as punishment.

**Ascalabus turned into a lizard**
While searching for Persephone, the thirsty Demeter drank a vessel of water (or barley drink) eagerly, and a boy named Ascalabus (or Abas in another version) mocked her. She splashed him with the drink and turned him into a spotted lizard (gecko).

**Iambe and Baubo**
Women who made the grieving Demeter laugh at Eleusis, Iambe with crude jokes and Baubo with an obscene gesture (in one version revealing the infant Iacchus). Their jests were commemorated in the ritual joking and the drinking of kykeon in Demeter's rites.

**Homeric Hymn to Demeter**
The main ancient source for Persephone's abduction, Demeter's stay at Eleusis, and the founding of the Eleusinian Mysteries. A second Homeric hymn to Demeter is only three lines long, one of the shortest in the collection.

**Epithets: Deo, Sito, Thesmophoros**
Demeter was also called Deo, Sito ("of the grain"), and Thesmophoros ("Law-Bringer"). The Mycenaean Linear B title si-to-po-ti-ni-ja ("Lady of the Grain") is thought to refer to an early form of her.
